summary_paraphrase: Every day after school Amo counts the six mielies in her grandmother's garden. One day there are five, then four; Koko guesses the birds Amo loves are eating them. Instead of chasing the birds away, Koko covers the cobs with cut plastic bottles, so the mielies are safe and the birds can still be watched.

beats.function: garden, birds, the daily count ritual, lunch with Koko
the count stops at five; recount
the birds she loves are the thieves
cobs safe, birds still there, at sunset

characters.name: Amo
characters.desire: to eat the mielies; to keep the birds
characters.fear: losing the mielies; having to chase the birds
characters.goal: find out where the mielies go
characters.problem: the count drops day by day
characters.change: from worry to relief that both loves can be kept

characters.name: Koko
characters.desire: lunch on time; a fair solution

characters.name: the birds
characters.relation_to_protagonist: loved creatures that turn out to be the thieves

humor_notes: No humor on the page; the book's pleasure is counting along and spotting the clues in the pictures.

repetition.description: Amo's call to the mielies before each count
repetition.why: it opens the ritual so the listener knows a count is coming

repetition.description: Counting the cobs aloud: to six, then breaking off at five, then at four
repetition.why: the pattern sets an expectation and its breaking is the plot; a child can count along and feel the gap

repetition.description: The call to lunch returns, once as a welcome and once as Koko's postponement
repetition.why: the second use carries mild tension, but it is easy to miss

notes: The culprit is in the pictures from the first spread: birds over the cobs, a bird's tail and spilled kernels on page 6, wings around the counting hand on page 7, feathers on page 9.
Plastic bottles stand on Koko's kitchen shelf on page 5, long before they become the solution on page 11.
The solution's mechanism (each cob inside a cut bottle) is shown only in the last picture.
Counting pages print the numerals large so a child can count along with the drawn cobs and fingers.

strengths: a counting pattern whose breaking is the plot
picture clues let a child solve the mystery before the adult names it
the solution keeps both loved things (mielies and birds) instead of chasing a 'villain'
very short sentences and a clear daily ritual
weaknesses: the adult finds and executes the solution; Amo only notices and asks
Koko postpones the problem once without reason

anti_patterns.note: Koko has the idea and the result; Amo's contribution is noticing and asking a humane question.
